tasks.title: First signal
tasks.statement: Connect input A to output Y with a plain wire. No gates are needed here: a wire can carry a signal too.
tasks.hint: Grab the round pin on the right of block A and drop it on the pin on the left of Y.

spec_text./success: The wire passes the signal unchanged: whatever goes in comes out. The table of all input combinations is the circuit's “passport”, and it is what we check against.

tasks.title: Inverter (NOT)
tasks.statement: Build a gate that flips the signal: output 1 when A = 0, and 0 when A = 1.
tasks.hint: The NOT gate has a single input. There is also a trick: a NOR with both inputs tied together is an inverter too.

spec_text./success: This is an inverter. Processors use inversion at every step, for example to test “not equal”. By the way, the NOR-based solution is accepted too!

tasks.title: AND gate
tasks.statement: Lamp Y lights up (1) only when BOTH inputs are 1.
tasks.hint: A single AND gate solves it: in “Goals” the only 1 is in the row 1 1.

spec_text./success: You built an AND gate. It works like two switches in series: current flows only if both are closed.

tasks.title: OR gate
tasks.statement: Lamp Y lights up when AT LEAST ONE input is 1.
tasks.hint: You can take a ready-made OR gate. Or build OR from AND and NOT: recall De Morgan's law, NOT(NOT-A AND NOT-B).

spec_text./success: This is OR, like two switches in parallel. A bonus for the curious: OR can be built from an AND and NOT gates, and that solution counts too.

tasks.title: NOR
tasks.statement: Lamp Y lights up only when BOTH inputs are 0.
tasks.hint: It is “NOT of OR”: first OR, then an inversion. Or use a single ready-made NOR gate.

spec_text./success: That is a NOR. Fun fact: an entire processor can be built from NOR gates alone (or from NAND alone).

tasks.title: NAND
tasks.statement: Lamp Y is always lit EXCEPT when both inputs are 1.
tasks.hint: “NOT of AND”: first an AND gate, then an inverter on its output.

spec_text./success: This is NAND, the “universal” gate. It is one of the cheapest on a chip, which is why whole integrated circuits used to be built from it alone.

tasks.title: Enable: letting a signal through
tasks.statement: D is data, E is enable. Only permitted data should reach the output: Y follows D, but only when E = 1; when E = 0 the output is always 0.
tasks.hint: It is still an AND gate: 1 only when both inputs are 1. Look closely: here E acts as a key and D as the data.

spec_text./success: An AND gate is not just “both sides agree”, it is also a KEY: the enable lets data through. This is how the enable input of a latch works (see the “D latch” exercise), so remember the trick.

tasks.title: Inhibit: a signal with a blocker
tasks.statement: Now the other way round: signal A passes only while B is SILENT. When B = 1 the output is always 0, whatever A does.
tasks.hint: First invert B with a NOT gate, then combine it with A through AND: Y = A AND NOT-B.

spec_text./success: This is an “inhibitor”: one signal allows, the other forbids. The circuit R = NOT-D·E at the D-latch input is exactly this fragment. The AND + NOT combination shows up all the time.

tasks.title: Unused inputs
tasks.statement: There are three inputs, but the circuit must react to A only: output 1 when A = 0, and 0 when A = 1. What to do with B and C is up to you.
tasks.hint: B and C can simply be left unconnected. An inverter is a NOT gate, or a NOR with tied inputs.

spec_text./success: B and C do not affect the output; such inputs are called “don't care”. Engineers simplify tables exactly this way: they cross out everything that does not matter.

tasks.title: Exclusive OR
tasks.statement: Lamp Y lights up when the inputs DIFFER: exactly one of the two is 1.
tasks.hint: Formula: (A OR B) AND NOT(A AND B). Build both parentheses as separate gates, then combine them with AND.

spec_text./formula: Y = (A OR B) AND NOT(A AND B)
spec_text./success: This is XOR, “addition modulo 2”. A one-bit adder inside a processor looks exactly like this: XOR adds the bits, and an AND gate produces the carry.

tasks.title: A pair: a signal and its shadow
tasks.statement: Build a circuit with TWO outputs: Y equals A AND B, and nY is its exact opposite (NOT(A AND B)). Check both columns of the table at once.
tasks.hint: One AND gate gives Y. Then pass Y through NOT to get nY. Attach the second wire directly to the output of the AND gate.

spec_text./success: Twin outputs Y and nY are called a “pair”. You will meet the pair Q and nQ in latches, and sum and carry in adders: one circuit, several answers.

tasks.title: Equality: comparing bits
tasks.statement: The lamp lights up when the inputs are the SAME: both 0 or both 1. This is the “A = B?” check, the basic comparison operation.
tasks.hint: Two ways: either NOT of XOR ((A OR B) AND NOT(A AND B), then NOT), or the direct formula (A AND B) OR (NOT-A AND NOT-B). If XNOR is already unlocked, there is a third: a single ready-made gate.

spec_text./success: This is XNOR, “exclusive NOR”, the equality gate. The ALU will compare bits this way. By finishing this exercise you unlocked a ready-made XNOR in the palette; build XOR too if you have not yet.

tasks.title: At least two
tasks.statement: The lamp lights up when AT LEAST TWO of the three inputs are 1. Such a circuit is called a majority circuit.
tasks.hint: Go through the three possible pairs: A AND B, or A AND C, or B AND C. Three AND gates, then two OR gates.

spec_text./formula: Y = AB OR AC OR BC
spec_text./success: A majority circuit “votes”: most of the inputs decide. It is used in reliability systems, for example when three sensors confirm a reading.

tasks.title: Multiplexer: choosing a channel
tasks.statement: A is the channel switch: when A = 0 the output carries signal B, when A = 1 it carries signal C.
tasks.hint: Two branches: (NOT-A AND B) and (A AND C), then OR. Check against the table: in the top half Y repeats B, in the bottom half it repeats C.

spec_text./success: You built a 2→1 multiplexer, a data-selection circuit. Multiplexers decide which data goes on through the processor. This is almost architecture already!
